units.label: page 2
units.text:
Life for Black people
• Post Civil War
• Life was difficult for Black people in the south
• Sharecropping
• Institutionalized racism
• Many moved north
• Other immigrants came from Caribbean

units.label: page 3
units.text:
Life for Black people
• Due to WWI, the migration of laborers from 
Europe almost completely stopped
• war resulted in a massive demand for unskilled 
industrial labor. 
• The Great Migration brought hundreds of 
thousands of Blacks to cities 
• Many African-American soldiers fought in 
segregated units such as the Harlem 
Hellfighters
• Came home to a nation did not respect them 
the same way as White vets
• Race riots during the Red Summer of 1919

units.label: page 4
units.text:
Harlem
• Originally developed in the 19th century 
as an exclusive suburb 
• Stately houses, grand avenues, 
• Polo Grounds 
• Harlem Opera House
• During massive immigration of Europeans 
in the late 19th century it was abandoned 
by the white middle class, who moved 
further north

units.label: page 5
units.text:
Claude McKay
• 1889-1948
• Born in Jamaica
• Educated by brother
• Studied in the US; Alabama and 
Kansas
• Travelled in Russia and France
• Moved to Harlem
• Wrote about homeland, social and 
political views of a Black man, love

units.label: page 6
units.text:
If we must die—let it not be like hogs
Hunted and penned in an inglorious spot,
While round us bark the mad and hungry dogs,
Making their mock at our accursed lot.
If we must die—oh, let us nobly die,
So that our precious blood may not be shed
In vain; then even the monsters we defy
Shall be constrained to honor us though dead!
Oh, Kinsmen!  We must meet the common foe;
Though far outnumbered, let us show us brave,
And for their thousand blows deal one deathblow!
What though before us lies the open grave?
Like men we’ll face the murderous, cowardly pack,
Pressed to the wall, dying, but fighting back
1919

units.label: page 7
units.text:
“If We Must Die” by 
Claude McKay
• Traditional Shakespearean sonnet
• ABAB CDCD EFEF GG
• Lines 1 - 4: speaker and his allies are under attack
• Don’t give up without a fight
• Lines 5 - 8: emotions of the allies to die honorably
• Lines 9 - 12: calls on allies to fight back even 
though they have no chance of winning. 
• Lines 13 - 14: even though we will die, we will die 
like men

units.label: page 8
units.text:
W . E. B. Du Bois
• 1868 – 1963, Massachusetts
• sociologist, historian, civil rights activist, Pan-Africanist, author, 
writer and editor
• University of Berlin and Harvard
• first Black person to earn a doctorate from Harvard
• one of the founders of the National Association for the Advancement 
of Colored People (NAACP)
• wrote one of the first scientific works in the American sociology
• Capitalism is a cause of racism; socialism is the answer

units.label: page 10
units.text:
Langston Hughes
• 1902-1967
• parents divorced; father 
moved to Mexico
• raised by grandmother
• moved to Cleveland, OH; 
started writing poetry
• gap year in Mexico
• Columbia University, NYC
• travelled to Africa and Europe
• One of the most influential 
black writers in history

units.label: page 11
units.text:
“Dreams” (1923)
Hold fast to dreams 
For if dreams die
Life is a broken-winged bird
That cannot fly.
Hold fast to dreams
For when dreams go
Life is a barren field
Frozen with snow.

units.label: page 12
units.text:
Thank You, M’am
Roger
• Poor
• Steals the purse
• Doesn’t run away
• Dynamic character:
• Roger changes in the story
• Learns that there are good people
Mrs. Luella Bates Washington Jones
• Not rich
• Doesn’t punish Roger 
• Feeds/talks to Roger
• Static character
• Doesn’t change in the story
• Has changed since she was 
young

units.label: page 13
units.text:
Adjectives to describe 
the characters
• Is there anything in the text about 
their race?
• Unlike other notable black writers of 
the period, Hughes did not see a 
difference between his personal 
experience and the experience of 
being black America 
• He told stories of (his) people in 
ways that reflected their actual 
culture
• suffering and their love of music, laughter, and 
language itself

units.label: page 14
units.text:
Making an 
argument 
What do you think?
• When someone mistreats you, you should still 
treat him/her with kindness and respect.
• People must always face the consequences of 
their actions.
• People are products of their environments. 
(The way you’re raised, your experiences, etc. 
determine the type of person you become.)
• There are no bad people—just bad choices.
